q: Which way of meeting the hardware moves a stream of bytes while the CPU is not involved at all?
choices: DMA
Interrupt
Polling
A critical section
why: With DMA the hardware itself moves the bytes. An interrupt still runs a CPU handler per event, and polling keeps the CPU busy asking.

q: According to the course, when is polling the right choice?
choices: When the wait is shorter than the cost of being interrupted
Never in real products; polling is only a beginner's shortcut for labs
When events are rare and must never be missed
When a long stream of data has to be moved
why: Polling is not the beginner option: if the wait is shorter than interrupt entry and exit, polling wins. Rare, must-not-miss events are the interrupt's case; streams are DMA's.

q: Which situation is the interrupt's natural use case?
choices: Events that are rare or must not be missed
Waits that are shorter than the interrupt entry cost
Moving a long block of bytes into RAM
Code that must never be preempted
why: Interrupts let the CPU do useful work until the hardware calls a handler, so rare or must-not-miss events fit best. Short waits suit polling; bulk transfers suit DMA.

q: Going from polling to interrupt to DMA, what happens to complexity and CPU time?
choices: Complexity rises, CPU time spent falls
Complexity falls, CPU time spent rises
Both complexity and CPU time rise
Both complexity and CPU time fall
why: Slide 1: cost rises left to right in complexity and falls in CPU time. Polling is simplest but burns the CPU; DMA frees the CPU but is the hardest to set up.

q: What is an interrupt on this Cortex-M0+, in the course's words?
choices: A hardware-forced function call between two instructions
A scheduler switching to another operating-system thread
A software call the main loop makes when it is ready
A jump that throws away main()'s register contents
why: No OS is involved: between two instructions the hardware stacks registers, looks up the vector and calls the handler. main()'s registers are saved, not lost.

q: How many registers does the hardware push automatically on interrupt entry?
why: Exactly eight words: r0–r3, r12, lr, pc and xPSR. It does not push all 16 registers; r4–r11 are left for the handler to save if it uses them.

q: Which set of registers does the hardware stack on interrupt entry?
choices: r0–r3, r12, lr, pc, xPSR
r4–r11, lr, pc
r0–r7 and the stack pointer
r0–r12, sp, lr, pc
why: The stacked set is r0–r3, r12, lr, pc, xPSR. r4–r11 are callee-saved, so an ordinary C function already preserves them.

q: Why can an ISR on this processor be an ordinary C function with no special keyword?
choices: The hardware stacks exactly the registers AAPCS lets a function destroy
The compiler adds a hidden interrupt prologue to every function
Cortex-M handlers are not allowed to use any registers at all
The linker wraps each handler in an assembly stub at build time
why: The eight stacked registers are the caller-saved set of AAPCS, and a C function preserves the rest itself. So no ISR() macro or keyword is needed.

q: On interrupt entry, what does the hardware write into IPSR?
choices: The exception number
The return address
The interrupt's priority level
The EXC_RETURN value
why: IPSR (the low bits of xPSR) gets the exception number, so the core knows what is running. The return address goes on the stack, and EXC_RETURN goes into LR.

q: What does LR hold when the handler starts, and how does the handler return?
choices: EXC_RETURN; an ordinary bx lr unstacks everything
The interrupted pc; a special reti instruction returns
Zero; the handler must pop pc from the stack itself
The handler's own address; the NVIC returns for it
why: The hardware loads LR with the special EXC_RETURN value, so a plain bx lr tells the core to unstack the frame and resume. There is no reti on Cortex-M.

q: SP is 0x20002F00 in main() when an interrupt arrives (assume no alignment padding). What is SP when the handler's first instruction runs?
why: Eight words are pushed: 8 × 4 = 32 = 0x20 bytes, and the stack grows down, so 0x20002F00 − 0x20 = 0x20002EE0. 0x20002F20 is the mistake of growing the stack up.

q: Which EXC_RETURN value means 'return to Thread mode on the main stack (MSP)'?
choices: 0xFFFFFFF9
0xFFFFFFFD
0xFFFFFFF1
0xFFFFFFFF
why: 0xFFFFFFF9 is Thread/MSP, which is what a bare-metal handler sees. 0xFFFFFFFD is Thread/PSP (an RTOS task), and 0xFFFFFFF1 returns to Handler mode.

q: You misspell an interrupt handler's name by one letter. What happens?
choices: It compiles and links cleanly; the interrupt never reaches your code
The compiler stops with an 'undefined handler' error
The linker warns that the vector entry is empty
The board takes a HardFault as soon as it boots
why: The name is the only connection to the vector table. A misspelt one is just an unused function: no error, no warning, and the interrupt does nothing useful.

q: What does the as-if rule allow a C compiler to do?
choices: Change anything as long as observable behaviour is the same
Nothing: it must run every statement exactly as written
Treat every global as volatile unless the programmer says otherwise
Reorder instructions only inside interrupt handlers
why: The compiler only has to produce the same observable behaviour as the source. How many times memory is read, or in what order, is otherwise free to change.

q: main() spins in while (flag == 0) {} waiting for an ISR to set flag, which is a plain (non-volatile) global. What does an optimising build do?
choices: Reads flag once and loops forever on a register
Reads flag every pass but in the wrong order
Refuses to compile, because flag is never written inside the loop
Exits the loop at once, assuming flag is already 1
why: Nothing inside the loop writes flag, so by C's rules it cannot change. The compiler reads it once and spins on the register copy: an infinite loop with no warning.

q: Why is the compiler allowed to optimise away the repeated reads of flag in a polling loop?
choices: Hardware and ISRs are observers that C knows nothing about
Optimisation at -Os is known to be buggy on Cortex-M
Globals are stored in flash, so they cannot change
An empty loop body is undefined behaviour in C
why: The language's idea of 'observable' does not include an ISR or a pin changing a variable. So by the rules the compiler is correct, not misbehaving.

q: What does declaring a variable volatile guarantee?
choices: Every access in the source is really performed, in order
Every access to it is atomic, even read-modify-write
Interrupts are masked whenever it is accessed
It is kept in a CPU register for fast access
why: volatile is about the compiler: every read and write written must really happen, in the order written. It does not make anything atomic and is not a lock.

q: Which of these does volatile NOT do?
choices: Make counter++ indivisible against an ISR
Force every read in the source to really happen
Keep the accesses in the order they were written
Stop the compiler caching the value in a register
why: The other three are exactly what volatile is for. It cannot make a load-add-store sequence indivisible; that needs a critical section.

q: On this load–store chip, what does counter++ on a global compile to?
choices: ldr, adds, str
A single add-to-memory instruction
ldr, str
adds, str
why: Only ldr/str touch memory, so the increment is load, add in a register, store back. The gap between ldr and str is where an interrupt can land.

q: counter = 5. main() executes ldr (reads 5); the ISR then runs, doing counter++; main() finishes adds and str. What is counter afterwards?
why: The ISR writes 6, then main() stores its stale 5 + 1 = 6 over it. Two increments happened, but one was lost.

q: counter = 10. Between main()'s ldr and str for counter++, the ISR fires three times and increments counter each time. Final value?
why: The ISR takes counter to 13, but main() then stores its stale 10 + 1 = 11. All three of the ISR's increments are wiped out.

q: counter is declared volatile and both main() and an ISR do counter++. Is the lost update fixed?
choices: No: it is still ldr, adds, str and the ISR can land in the gap
Yes: volatile makes the increment a single atomic access
Yes: volatile stops the ISR from running during the access
No: an ISR is not allowed to write a volatile variable
why: volatile only ensures each access really happens. The sequence is still three instructions and can be split, so you need a critical section.

q: counter = 7. main() runs counter++ and is interrupted between ldr and str by an ISR that does counter--. What is counter afterwards?
why: One increment and one decrement should leave 7. But main() stores its stale 7 + 1 = 8 over the ISR's 6, so the decrement is lost.

q: What is a race condition?
choices: The result depends on the relative timing of two contexts
Two interrupts of equal priority arriving in the same clock cycle
A loop that runs faster than the hardware can respond
A stack that grows into the heap
why: A race condition is any result that depends on the relative timing of two contexts. It is general computing vocabulary, not ARM-specific.

q: What is a critical section?
choices: Code that must not be interleaved with another context
The part of the vector table that is reserved for the fault handlers
An interrupt handler with the highest priority
A section in link.ld that must be placed in RAM
why: A critical section is a stretch of code that must not be interleaved. Mutual exclusion is the guarantee you need over it.

q: What does mutual exclusion guarantee?
choices: At most one context is inside the critical section at a time
Each shared variable is written by exactly one context, never two
Interrupts are delivered in priority order
Two contexts never share any global variable
why: Mutual exclusion means at most one context inside the critical section at once. It does not forbid sharing; it controls when the shared code runs.

q: An operation is called atomic when it…
choices: cannot be observed half-done
runs in exactly one clock cycle
is marked volatile in the source
is executed by the DMA controller
why: Atomic means no other context can see the operation half-finished. A single aligned store is atomic on this chip; a read-modify-write is not.

q: What is tearing?
choices: A reader takes one value in two accesses and gets half old, half new
Two ISRs writing the same peripheral register in the same bus cycle
A stack overflow that corrupts the vector table
An interrupt lost because PRIMASK was set too long
why: Tearing happens when one logical value needs two bus accesses and a writer runs in between. The result is a number nobody ever stored.

q: ISR versus main() on one core: how do you get mutual exclusion?
choices: Mask interrupts around the critical section
Declare the shared variable volatile so both sides see each write
Use an OS mutex inside the ISR
Raise the ISR to NVIC priority 0
why: If interrupts are off, the ISR cannot start, so it cannot interleave. volatile does not give exclusion, and an ISR cannot block on a mutex.

q: Two threads under one operating system share a variable. What is the usual mutual-exclusion tool?
choices: A mutex: the scheduler won't switch to the waiter
Masking interrupts on the current core
Declaring the variable volatile
An atomic ldrex/strex retry loop around every access
why: Between threads on one OS, a mutex asks the scheduler not to run the waiter until the owner unlocks. Masking interrupts is the ISR-versus-main tool.

q: A dual-core chip: core 0 calls __disable_irq() before updating a counter that core 1 also updates. Is the counter protected?
choices: No: core 1 keeps running; an atomic read-modify-write is needed
Yes: cpsid i stops every core on the chip, not just this one
Yes, as long as the counter is declared volatile
No: you need to mask interrupts on core 1 instead
why: Masking only stops other contexts on this core. Across cores you need an atomic read-modify-write such as ldrex/strex or x86 lock cmpxchg.

q: Why is masking interrupts the right lock on this course's chip but the wrong one on a phone?
choices: The Cortex-M0+ has a single core, and no ldrex/strex either
Phones have no interrupts, only DMA
PRIMASK only exists on multi-core chips
The M0+ runs too slowly for a mutex
why: On one core, masking stops the only other context. A phone has several cores, and masking on one does nothing to the others.

q: Which instruction does __disable_irq() compile to?
choices: cpsid i
cpsie i
svc #0
wfi
why: __disable_irq() is cpsid i and __enable_irq() is cpsie i. Each is a single instruction that changes PRIMASK bit 0.

q: Right after __disable_irq(), what does PRIMASK read?
choices: 0xFF
why: PRIMASK has one bit, PM at bit 0. cpsid i sets it to 1, which masks every configurable interrupt; 0 is the reset state, with interrupts on.

q: Why must critical sections be kept short?
choices: The longest one sets the worst-case interrupt latency
The compiler cannot optimise code inside them
PRIMASK clears itself automatically after 1 ms
Interrupts that arrive while masked are discarded
why: While interrupts are off the chip cannot respond to anything, so the longest critical section bounds latency. Masked interrupts stay pending; they are delayed, not discarded.

q: What is interrupt latency?
choices: The time from the hardware event to the handler's first instruction
The time a handler takes from entry to bx lr
The time between two interrupts of the same source
The delay of the debounce filter after a press
why: Latency is the gap between the event and the start of your handler. Critical sections and higher-priority handlers add to it.

q: The longest critical section in a program is 960 cycles at 48 MHz. What is the worst-case latency it adds?
choices: 20 µs
2 µs
46 µs
200 µs
why: 960 / 48 000 000 = 20 µs. 46 µs is what you get by multiplying 960 × 48 instead of dividing.

q: 'Two fixes, two problems.' Which pairing is correct?
choices: volatile makes accesses real; a critical section makes a sequence indivisible
volatile makes a sequence indivisible; a critical section makes accesses real
volatile and a critical section both make accesses atomic
volatile prevents tearing; a critical section prevents caching
why: volatile stops the compiler removing or caching accesses. A critical section stops another context splitting a sequence. They are not interchangeable.

q: According to the course, most concurrency bugs come from which mistake?
choices: Using volatile where a critical section was needed
Using a critical section where volatile was needed
Giving the ISR too high an NVIC priority
Polling where an interrupt was needed
why: Students add volatile, the lost update remains, and they conclude the language is broken. The sequence needed to be made indivisible.

q: A handler must finish within 10 µs at 48 MHz. How many cycles is that budget?
why: 48 000 000 cycles/s × 10 µs = 480 cycles. 4800 is the 100 µs budget.

q: How wide is the window in which an interrupt causes a lost update to counter++ at 48 MHz?
choices: About 40 ns
About 4 µs
About 1 ms
About 400 ns
why: The interrupt must land in a two-instruction gap. At 48 MHz that is roughly 40 nanoseconds.

q: At 48 MHz, how long is one clock cycle?
choices: About 20.8 ns
About 48 ns
About 2.08 ns
About 208 ns
why: 1 / 48 000 000 s ≈ 20.8 ns. Two instructions take about 40 ns, which is the lost-update window.

q: With 1000 interrupts per second, roughly how often does the counter++ lost update appear?
choices: About once every 7 hours
About once a second
About once every 7 minutes
About once a week
why: The 40 ns window is tiny, so at 1000 interrupts per second the bug shows up only about once every 7 hours. That is why it survives testing.

q: A lost update appears about once every 7 hours at 1000 interrupts/s. Roughly how often at 10 000 interrupts/s?
choices: About every 40 minutes
About every 70 hours
About every 7 minutes
About every 4 minutes
why: Ten times more interrupts means about ten times more chances: 7 h / 10 ≈ 42 min, which the slide rounds to 40 minutes.

q: A program works for hours, then misbehaves once. How do you find a race condition like this?
choices: Reason about which variables more than one context touches
Run the test overnight until it fails again
Add printf calls inside the interrupt handler to trace the timing
Build with optimisation turned off
why: You can't find it by running more: the window is nanoseconds wide. You list every global, note which contexts touch it, and protect the shared ones.

q: The course's discipline for globals: if more than one context touches a variable, it needs…
choices: volatile, and probably a critical section too
a critical section only; volatile is optional
nothing, if it is a 32-bit variable
to be moved into the ISR as a local
why: Shared means volatile so accesses really happen, and usually a critical section so sequences are not split. The exceptions are on the 'what needs protection' table.

q: The lost update shows up about once every 7 hours at 1000 interrupts/s. Roughly how often at 100 interrupts/s?
choices: About every 70 hours
About every 40 minutes
About every 7 hours
About every 42 minutes
why: Ten times fewer interrupts means about ten times fewer chances to hit the window: 7 h × 10 = 70 h. A rarer bug is harder to catch, not safer.

q: The ISR writes a single aligned 32-bit word and main() only reads it. Safe without a critical section?
choices: Yes: one access, one writer, so it can't tear
No: every shared variable needs a critical section
No: main() can read half of the word while the ISR is writing it
Only if the ISR has priority 3
why: A single aligned word is one bus access, and only one context writes it. main() sees the old value or the new one, never a mix.

q: The ISR sets a flag; main() reads it and then clears it. How safe is this?
choices: Usually safe, but the clear is a read-modify-write
Always safe, because the flag is a single byte
Never safe, because the ISR writes it
Safe only if the flag is uint64_t
why: Setting from one side and clearing from the other mostly works, but the clear is itself load-modify-store. If the ISR sets it again inside that gap, a set can be lost.

q: An ISR writes a uint64_t timestamp and main() only reads it. There is only one writer. Safe?
choices: No: two 32-bit accesses, so main() can read a torn value
Yes: a single writer is always safe
Yes, as soon as the timestamp is declared volatile
No: an ISR cannot write 64-bit variables
why: 'One writer' is only safe for a single aligned word. A 64-bit value takes two bus accesses on a 32-bit machine, so the reader can get half old and half new.

q: A uint64_t goes from 0x00000000FFFFFFFF to 0x0000000100000000. main() reads the low word, the ISR updates the value, then main() reads the high word. What does main() get?
choices: 0x00000001FFFFFFFF
0x00000000FFFFFFFF
why: Low word from before (0xFFFFFFFF), high word from after (0x00000001): 0x00000001FFFFFFFF, a value that was never stored. That is tearing.

q: An ISR updates a struct with x, y and a timestamp; main() reads all three. Safe?
choices: No: main() can see the struct half-updated
Yes: each field on its own is small enough to be read atomically
Yes, as long as the struct is declared volatile
Only if each field is written in address order
why: Each field may be atomic, but the struct as a whole is several accesses. A reader in the middle sees new x with old y: tearing at the struct level.

q: A global uint32_t is written only by an ISR and only read by main(). What does it need?
choices: volatile, but no critical section
A critical section, but no volatile
Both volatile and a critical section
Neither, because it is one word
why: volatile makes main() really reload it each time. It needs no critical section: one aligned word with one writer can't tear.

q: A shared uint8_t is written only by the ISR and only read by main(). Does it need a critical section?
choices: No: a single aligned byte access with one writer can't be split
Yes: anything shared with an ISR needs one
Yes: bytes are read as part of a 32-bit word
No, but only if the ISR runs at priority 0
why: A byte is one access, and with only one writer there is nothing to interleave. It still needs volatile so main() really reads it.

q: How many NVIC priority levels does this chip have, and which is most urgent?
choices: 4 levels; 0 is the most urgent
4 levels; 3 is the most urgent
256 levels; 0 is the most urgent
16 levels; 15 is the most urgent
why: Only the top 2 bits of each 8-bit priority field exist, giving 4 levels. In the NVIC a lower number is more urgent.

q: Which byte value sets an IRQ to NVIC priority 3?
choices: 0xC0
0x0C
why: Only bits 7:6 of the byte exist, so the value is prio << 6 = 3 << 6 = 0xC0. Writing 0x03 lands in bits that don't exist.

q: An IRQ's priority byte reads 0x80. What priority level is it?
why: The level is the top two bits: 0x80 = 1000 0000, so bits 7:6 = 10 = 2. Only those two bits are implemented.

q: Code writes 0x03 straight into IRQ 4's priority byte, meaning 'least urgent'. What level does IRQ 4 actually get?
choices: 0, the most urgent
3, the least urgent
It faults on the write
why: The low six bits don't exist and read as 0, so 0x03 becomes 0x00: level 0, the most urgent. The value needs shifting: 3 << 6 = 0xC0.

q: IRQ 2 is given priority 1 and every other IRQ in IPR[0] is 0. What does IPR[0] read?
why: IRQ 2 is byte 2 of IPR[0] (bits 23:16). Its value is 1 << 6 = 0x40, so 0x40 << 16 = 0x00400000. 0x00004000 would be IRQ 1's byte.

q: A timer handler is running when a more urgent interrupt arrives. What happens?
choices: The urgent one preempts the timer handler, which resumes afterwards
The urgent one waits until the timer handler returns
The timer handler is aborted and its work discarded
Both handlers run at once on the same core
why: The NVIC lets a more urgent interrupt preempt a running handler. That also means sharing is now ISR versus ISR, not only ISR versus main().

q: Why must interrupt handlers be short?
choices: A slow handler delays every interrupt of equal or lower priority
Handlers longer than 32 instructions corrupt the stacked frame
The NVIC aborts any handler that runs over 1 ms
Long handlers stop main() from using volatile
why: While a handler runs, equal and lower-priority interrupts wait. The usual shape is: set a flag or buffer the data, return, and let main() do the work.

q: What is priority inversion?
choices: A high-priority task waits, in effect, on a lower-priority one
Priority 0 being most urgent instead of priority 3
Two interrupts with equal priority firing at once
A handler lowering its own priority to finish sooner
why: In priority inversion an urgent task is stuck waiting on something a low-priority task holds. It is introduced in lesson 03 and covered fully in lesson 07.

q: Which famous system kept resetting because of priority inversion?
choices: Mars Pathfinder, 1997
Apollo 11, 1969
Ariane 5, 1996
Therac-25, 1985
why: Mars Pathfinder kept resetting on the surface of Mars in 1997 because of priority inversion. Ariane 5 failed from an overflow, and Therac-25 from a race in its software.

q: Suppose a chip implemented the top 3 bits of each priority byte instead of 2. How many priority levels would it have?
why: n implemented bits give 2^n levels: 2 bits give this chip's 4, and 3 bits would give 8. The count doubles per bit; it does not go up by 2.

q: IRQ 0 gets priority 1 and IRQ 1 gets priority 2; IRQs 2 and 3 are left at 0. What does IPR[0] read?
why: IRQ 0 is byte 0: 1 << 6 = 0x40. IRQ 1 is byte 1: 2 << 6 = 0x80, shifted 8 bits to 0x8000. Together that is 0x00008040; 0x00004080 swaps the two bytes.
